    `WithAuthz()` beside `WithoutDefaults()`. The default-deny enforcer
    loads the policy file and the module rows and gates the metrics path;
    the bearer is decoded ahead of the API-key read, the limiter and the
    interceptors; nothing else of the default stack is built.
  - The application should authorize its routes and wants the rest of the
    default stack too: remove `WithoutDefaults()`. The default stack also
    builds mail (the `noop` driver unless one is declared), the local
    storage default and the rate limiter.
  - The application authorizes in its handlers, or not at all: remove
    `rbac_policy_file` and `metrics_public: false`, and keep the metrics
    path private at the network layer.
  - A module of the application's own declares rows: `WithAuthz()`, or
    remove them and refuse the callers in the module's own middleware or
    handlers. A module the application does not own — its rows cannot be
    removed from the composition root — needs `WithAuthz()` or the default
    stack. A module `nucleus generate module` wrote on such a root declares
    none: its rows are commented out until `WithAuthz()` is added (see
    Notes).
- Behavior differences: with `WithAuthz()`, as on the default stack, every
  route answers only to the callers a policy grants; a route nobody granted
  answers 403. With no policy file and no module rows that is every
  registered route outside the bootstrap allow-list (`/healthz`, `/livez`,
  `/readyz`, `/login`, `/.well-known/jwks.json`, `/static/*`, and
  `/metrics` unless `metrics_public: false`), and the boot log says so:
  `authz: default-deny with 0 policy rows`.
- Required app changes: one builder call added (or `WithoutDefaults()`
  removed) and a policy reviewed, or two keys deleted.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-017-ignored-authz-config-to-default-stack.md`
- Detection rule: the boot log lines `authz configuration IGNORED` and
  `module policies DISCARDED` carrying `deprecation="DEP-2026-017…"`, or the
  `nucleus doctor --check rbac` warning naming this notice.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — the choice between the two paths above is the
  application's.

### DEP-2026-018 — the profiler served unguarded by an application built WithoutDefaults() without WithAuthz() → refused at v2.0.0 unless WithAuthz() guards it

*change · scope `config` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-02 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-018-unguarded-profiler-without-defaults.md`*

**What changes**

`profiling_enabled: true` mounts `net/http/pprof` under `/debug/pprof`: the
index, `cmdline`, `profile`, `symbol`, `trace`, and the named profiles —
`heap` and `goroutine` among them. A heap dump is not a summary: it carries
the process's live memory, session tokens, credentials and request payloads
included. That is why the profiler is off by default and deliberately not in
the anonymous bootstrap allow-list: on the default stack the default-deny
enforcer answers an anonymous request `403`, and only a policy that grants
the paths opens them.

An application built `WithoutDefaults()` builds no enforcer unless it also
carries `WithAuthz()`. Without it, with the profiler on, it served those
dumps to anyone who reached the port, unless the application's own
middleware refused them, and the boot log carried a WARN telling the
operator to "keep it behind a policy" that such an application cannot have.

The application keeps serving the profiler, as before, and now says so in
one ERROR line at boot instead of the WARN. `WithAuthz()` puts the profiler
behind the default stack's default-deny gate: `403` to an anonymous
request, and the default stack's WARN instead of the ERROR.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** the combination is reported, not refused. The boot log
  carries, once:

  ```
  level=ERROR msg="profiler UNGUARDED: profiling_enabled mounts /debug/pprof and this application is built WithoutDefaults() without WithAuthz(), which builds no RBAC enforcer, so no policy can say who may read it — heap and goroutine dumps answer anyone who reaches the port, unless the application's own middleware refuses them" prefix=/debug/pprof env=development fix="add WithAuthz() beside WithoutDefaults() — nucleus.New().FromConfigFile(\"nucleus.yml\").WithoutDefaults().WithAuthz(), or app.New(cfg, app.WithoutDefaults(), app.WithAuthz()) — and grant /debug/pprof/* to an on-call role in the policy, never to anonymous; or set profiling_enabled: false, and serve net/http/pprof from a listener only operators reach when you need a profile" deprecation="DEP-2026-018: from v2.0.0 this configuration refuses to start unless WithAuthz() guards the profiler"
  ```

  Under `env: production` the message names the stake outright —
  `profiler UNGUARDED in production: … anyone who reaches the port can
  download heap dumps of this production process, with the live memory they
  carry (session tokens, credentials, request payloads) …`.

  `nucleus doctor --check security` reports the same combination when it
  finds the composition root beside the configuration and the root does not
  call `WithAuthz()`: a **high-risk setting** (error) in production, a
  setting to review (warning) elsewhere. Without a root to read — a
  deployed image carries the binary, not `main.go` — it says the profiler
  is guarded only on the default stack or with `WithAuthz()`, instead of
  implying it is.

- **v2.0.0:** an application built `WithoutDefaults()` with
  `profiling_enabled: true` refuses to start, with the same message as the
  error, unless `WithAuthz()` guards the profiler — the explicit opt-in the
  refusal accepts (see Notes).

**How to migrate**

- Replacement, by intent:
  - The application should authorize its routes against a policy, and stay
    core-only: add `WithAuthz()` beside `WithoutDefaults()`, and grant
    `/debug/pprof/*` to an on-call role, never to `anonymous`. Every other
    route then answers only to the callers a policy grants as well.
  - The application does not need the profiler in this deployment: set
    `profiling_enabled: false` (the default).
  - The application needs a profile now and then: serve `net/http/pprof`
    yourself from a listener only operators reach — `127.0.0.1:6060`, or a
    port the network does not route — rather than on the application's
    public port.
  - The application wants the rest of the default stack too: build it with
    the defaults — remove `WithoutDefaults()` — and grant `/debug/pprof/*`
    to an on-call role, never to `anonymous`.
- Behavior differences: with `WithAuthz()`, as on the default stack, every
  route, not only the profiler, answers only to the callers a policy
  grants.
- Required app changes: one builder call added and a policy reviewed, or
  one key, or a few lines that start a private listener, or one builder
  call removed and a policy reviewed.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-018-unguarded-profiler-to-private-listener.md`
- Detection rule: the boot log line `profiler UNGUARDED` carrying
  `deprecation="DEP-2026-018…"`, or the `nucleus doctor --check security`
  finding naming this notice.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — the choice between the paths above is the
  application's.

### DEP-2026-019 — `nucleustest` stops linking SQLite into every test binary at v2.0.0

*change · scope `api` (test support)` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-019-nucleustest-links-sqlite.md`*

**What changes**

`pkg/nucleustest` imports `modernc.org/sqlite` for its side effect
(`runtime.go`), so `TempSQLite` and `CheckModule` work in a test binary that
imports no database driver of its own. The price is paid by every test
binary that imports `nucleustest`: it links the pure-Go SQLite engine whether
the application under test uses SQLite or not — measured in A12 `N1` as the
one dependency `nucleustest` carries into production code (NU-121). The
framework moved its own tests off that import in `v1.32.0`
(`internal/testsqlite`); the public helper could not follow without
breaking the tests that rely on it, so it waits for the major.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** nothing. `nucleustest` keeps linking SQLite; this notice
  and the pinned test say so.
- **v2.0.0:** `nucleustest` imports no driver. `TempSQLite` keeps existing and
  returns the same configuration; opening it fails with a message that names
  the import to add when no `sqlite` driver is registered. A test that uses
  another engine imports that engine's driver module instead and links no
  SQLite.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: add the blank import in one `_test.go` file of each package
  that uses the helper:

  ```go
  import _ "github.com/jcsvwinston/nucleus/drivers/sqlite"
  ```

  A test written this way behaves the same before and after 2.0.
- Behavior differences: none in v1. At v2.0.0 a test binary without the
  import fails at the first `TempSQLite`-backed call with the import named.
- Required app changes: one import line per test package that relies on the
  helper's implicit driver.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-019-nucleustest-import-your-driver.md`
- Detection rule: a test package that imports `pkg/nucleustest` and no
  `drivers/*` module (`grep -L 'nucleus/drivers/' $(grep -l 'pkg/nucleustest' -r --include='*_test.go' .)`).
- Suggested rewrite: manual — the blank import above.

### DEP-2026-020 — the asynq jobs provider moves to `providers/tasks-asynq` at v2.0.0

*change · scope `packaging` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-020-asynq-provider-to-its-own-module.md`*

**What changes**

`pkg/tasks/providers/asynq` is the Redis-backed jobs provider, selected with
`jobs_provider: asynq`. It lives in the framework's root module, so
`github.com/hibiken/asynq` and its Redis client are in the `go.mod` of every
application, whether it runs jobs on Redis or not. The memory and SQL
providers need no broker; asynq is the one that brings a client library with
it, and the A12 `S0` measurement of the hello-world graph listed it among the
dependencies the core carries for a feature most applications do not turn on.

What changes and when:

- **The announcing release:** nothing. The provider stays where it is; this
  notice says where it goes.
- **The next minor after `v1.34.0`:** the module
  `github.com/jcsvwinston/nucleus/providers/tasks-asynq` exists, as a
  forwarding module: it imports `pkg/tasks/providers/asynq` and re-exports
  its whole surface (the types as aliases, the same error values, thin
  constructors), and `contracts/tasks_asynq_module_test.go` holds the two
  surfaces equal. `nucleus add tasks-asynq` and the blank import work from
  that minor on; the framework still links the provider, so the import is
  optional until the major and nothing else changes. An application that
  writes it now has only the version to change at v2.0.0.
- **v2.0.0:** the provider lives in its own module,
  `github.com/jcsvwinston/nucleus/providers/tasks-asynq`, with its own tag,
  like the drivers, exporters and the other providers (ADR-030/031). The
  package path and every exported symbol keep their names inside the new
  module. An application that selects `jobs_provider: asynq` without the
  module linked fails at boot with the guided error the other optional
  modules already use, naming `nucleus add tasks-asynq`.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: `nucleus add tasks-asynq`, available since the forwarding
  module's first minor and required at the upgrade, (or a blank import of
  the new module in the composition root) and the import path
  `github.com/jcsvwinston/nucleus/providers/tasks-asynq` for code that names
  the provider's symbols.
- Behavior differences: none. Same provider, same configuration keys, same
  behaviour.
- Required app changes: one `go get`/`nucleus add` and, where the package is
  imported directly, the import path.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-020-asynq-provider-module.md`
- Detection rule: `jobs_provider: asynq` in the configuration or
  `NUCLEUS_JOBS_PROVIDER=asynq`; a direct import of
  `pkg/tasks/providers/asynq`.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — `nucleus add tasks-asynq`; `sed` on the import
  path.

### DEP-2026-021 — `session_idle_timeout` ships as 30m at v2.0.0

*change · scope `config` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-021-session-idle-timeout-default.md`*

**What changes**

`session_idle_timeout` is honoured and ships disabled: its default is `0`, so
a session that is never used again stays valid for its whole
`session_lifetime` (72 hours by default). `nucleus doctor security` warns
about the `0` in production and ASVS V3.3.2 asks for an inactivity timeout.
Turning it on by default in a minor would start expiring sessions in every
deployment that upgrades, which is why it waited for the major (NU-72,
QADR-0010).

What changes and when:

- **This release:** nothing. The default stays `0`; this notice and the pinned
  test say so.
- **v2.0.0:** the default becomes `30m` — what `docs/guides/AUTH_GUIDE.md`
  shows and what `doctor security` asks for. A session with no request for
  30 minutes expires, whatever its lifetime says. An explicit
  `session_idle_timeout: 0` keeps the behaviour of today: the loader applies
  the struct defaults first and the configuration file on top, so a zero
  written in the file survives a non-zero default (pinned by
  `TestLoadConfig_AnExplicitZeroSurvivesANonZeroDefault`).

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: decide the value before the upgrade and write it down. To keep
  today's behaviour: `session_idle_timeout: 0`. To adopt the new default
  early and stop `doctor security` asking: `session_idle_timeout: 30m`.
- Behavior differences: at v2.0.0 an application that sets nothing expires
  idle sessions after 30 minutes; its users sign in again after a pause.
- Required app changes: one configuration key, or none to accept the default.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-021-session-idle-timeout.md`
- Detection rule: `nucleus doctor security` reporting `session_idle_timeout=0`
  (an explicit zero shows the same warning; it is the intended choice when
  written); a configuration without the key.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — one key.

### DEP-2026-022 — RFC 9457 problem details become the default error shape at v2.0.0

*change · scope `api` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-022-problem-details-default-error-shape.md`*

**What changes**

Every error an application answers — a handler's error, a binding failure,
the router's 404 and 405, a timeout, the refusals of the CSRF middleware, the
rate limiter, the authorizer and the bearer middleware — is written in the
framework's envelope:

```json
{"error": {"code": "NOT_FOUND", "message": "no route serves GET /api/nope"}}
```

A client that prefers `application/problem+json` in its `Accept` header gets
RFC 9457 problem details instead, and an application can make problem details
the shape for every client with `WithProblemDetails()` (A10). The envelope is
a shape of this framework; problem details are the standard one, and the
derived OpenAPI document already describes both. The owner decided that the
standard shape becomes the default at the major.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** the way to keep the envelope is added — `WithErrorEnvelope()`
  (`app.WithErrorEnvelope`, `nucleus.WithErrorEnvelope`,
  `AppBuilder.WithErrorEnvelope`), the opposite of `WithProblemDetails()`.
  It changes nothing today: the envelope is the default either way, and
  `App.ErrorEnvelope()` reports the choice. Passing both options is refused
  by `app.New`.
- **v2.0.0:** an application that passes neither option answers every error
  as `application/problem+json`. An application built with
  `WithErrorEnvelope()` keeps the envelope; a client of it that negotiates
  problem details through `Accept` still gets them, as today.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: choose the shape in code, before the upgrade.
  - Keep today's shape: `nucleus.New().WithErrorEnvelope()` (or
    `app.New(cfg, app.WithErrorEnvelope())`).
  - Adopt the standard shape early: `nucleus.New().WithProblemDetails()`.
  - Clients that must work with either: read `Content-Type` and parse
    `application/problem+json` (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`,
    `instance`, plus `code` and `details` as extension members) beside the
    envelope.
- Behavior differences: at v2.0.0 an application that chose nothing answers
  problem details; status codes do not change; `code` is still present, as an
  extension member.
- Required app changes: one builder call, or none to accept the new default.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-022-error-shape-choose-in-code.md`
- Detection rule: a composition root with neither `WithProblemDetails()` nor
  `WithErrorEnvelope()`; `App.ProblemDetails()` and `App.ErrorEnvelope()`
  both false at run time.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — one option.

### DEP-2026-023 — `router.NewWrapResponseWriter(w, protoMajor)` → `router.Wrap(w)`

*removal · scope `api` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-023-newwrapresponsewriter-replaced-by-wrap.md`*

**What changes**

`router.NewWrapResponseWriter(w http.ResponseWriter, protoMajor int)` wraps a
response writer to record the status code and the bytes written. Its second
argument was accepted for compatibility with chi's constructor of the same
name and has never been read (NU-41, audit of 2026-09-03). A parameter a
function ignores is a promise it does not keep; the replacement takes only
the writer.

This release adds `router.Wrap(w)` and marks the old constructor
`// Deprecated:`; the framework's own callers (the logging middleware, the
OpenTelemetry middleware and the HTTP observability hook) use `Wrap`.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: `router.Wrap(w)`.

  ```go
  // before
  ww := router.NewWrapResponseWriter(w, r.ProtoMajor)
  // after
  ww := router.Wrap(w)
  ```

- Behavior differences: none — the old constructor calls the new one.
- Required app changes: the call site.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-023-wrap-response-writer.md`
- Detection rule: `grep -rn 'NewWrapResponseWriter(' --include='*.go'`;
  staticcheck SA1019 on the marker.
- Suggested rewrite: automatic —
  `sed -E 's/NewWrapResponseWriter\(([^,]+), [^)]+\)/Wrap(\1)/g'`.

### DEP-2026-024 — `pkg/model` leaves the public API at v2.0.0

*removal · scope `api` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-024-pkg-model-leaves-the-public-api.md`*

**What changes**

`pkg/model` is the framework's own data layer: a registry of models
(`Registry`, `ModelMeta`, `FieldMeta`), reflection-based metadata, a generic
`CRUD` over `database/sql`, migration scaffolds per engine and lifecycle
signals. It predates Quark. Quark is the data layer of the suite (A4, A8),
and keeping a second one in the framework means two tag vocabularies that
disagree about what `db` means (the umbrella's finding «las dos capas de
datos se contradicen»), two ways to write a model in the documentation, and
a starter that teaches the one the suite does not recommend.

The owner decided on 2026-10-16 that `pkg/model` leaves the public API with
the major — not that it is demoted and kept — and that the Orbit adapter
built on it (`datasource/nucleus`) leaves with it, so that the admin panel
reads Quark models only (`quarkdatasource`). The 48 exported symbols of the
package are marked `// Deprecated:` in this release; nothing is removed in
v1.x.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** the package, `BaseModel`, `NewRegistry` and `NewCRUD`
  carry the marker; everything keeps working. At the time of this notice
  `nucleus generate model` and `nucleus generate resource` still produced
  `pkg/model`, and `nucleustest`'s factories used it; `nucleus generate
  module` already built on Quark. Moving the rest to Quark is the «DX al 5»
  work of the suite's 2.0 contract (§2.1), additive, in 1.x minors before the
  major — done for the generators and the factory in NU-137: `generate
  model`, `generate resource` and `startapp` write a Quark model and a Quark
  repository, and `nucleustest.Make` persists a Quark model through Quark by
  way of the `pkg/nucleustest/quarkmake` module, installed with
  `srv.UseFactory` (D12: the framework's `go.mod` keeps Quark out of its
  graph; a registered `pkg/model` model keeps its path until v2.0.0).
- **v2.0.0:** `pkg/model` is no longer part of the public API. What the
  framework still needs internally — the migration scaffolds the generators
  render, the SQL observer — moves under `internal/`. `Runtime.Models()` and
  `App.Models` go with the registry. Applications define their models with
  Quark and register them with the application the way the starter of that
  release does.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: a Quark model (`quark.For[T]`, `quark:"..."` tags) and Quark's
  hooks for what the lifecycle signals did. The suite documents the pairing
  in Nucleus' «Using Quark with Nucleus» and in Quark's `init --with nucleus`.
- Behavior differences: Quark checks versions, scopes tenants and escapes
  `LIKE` by its own rules; the migration is a rewrite of the model layer, not
  a rename. The generators produce the Quark form since NU-137.
- Required app changes: model definitions, the handlers that call
  `model.CRUD`, and tests that use `nucleustest`'s factories over
  `pkg/model`.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-024-pkg-model-to-quark.md`
- Detection rule: `grep -rln 'nucleus/pkg/model"' --include='*.go'`;
  staticcheck SA1019 on the package.
- Suggested rewrite: manual, with `nucleus generate model <Name>` as the
  reference for the target form.

### DEP-2026-025 — the untyped door of `pkg/signals` leaves at v2.0.0

*removal · scope `api` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-025-signals-untyped-door.md`*

**What changes**

`signals.Bus` is one bus with two doors. The typed one, delivered by A7
(`Define`, `Topic[T]`, `Subscribe`, `Publish`, `PublishAsync`), carries the
payload as the type its topic declares and the context the event was
published with. The untyped one — `Signal`, `Event{Payload any}`, `Handler`,
`Bus.On`, `Bus.Emit`, `Bus.EmitAsync` — moves `any`: every handler asserts
the type it hopes for, and a producer that changes its payload breaks its
subscribers at run time, one event at a time. A7 kept both because
`signals.Event` was published and QADR-0010 holds breaking changes for the
major. The major is where the untyped door closes.

The built-in lifecycle names (`PreCreate` … `PostUpdate`) are emitted by
`pkg/model`, which leaves the public API with the same major (DEP-2026-024);
they leave with it and are not replaced by typed topics.
`observability.Bus` is a different thing — the in-process fan-out of
observability events — and does not change.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** `Signal`, the lifecycle constants, `Event`, `Handler`,
  `Bus.On`, `Bus.Emit`, `Bus.EmitAsync` and `Topic.Name` carry
  `// Deprecated:`; `Topic.String()` is added as the way to read a topic's
  name without the `Signal` type. Everything keeps working, and a typed
  publish still reaches untyped subscribers of the same name and the other
  way round.
- **v2.0.0:** the untyped symbols are removed. `Bus.Clear` takes topic names
  as strings. The Redis relay and the outbox bridge, which feed the bus, use
  an internal publish.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement, for an application's own events:

  ```go
  // before
  bus.On("invoice.paid", func(e signals.Event) error {
      p := e.Payload.(InvoicePaid) // asserts, or panics
      return mail(e.Ctx, p)
  })
  _ = bus.Emit(signals.Event{Signal: "invoice.paid", Payload: InvoicePaid{...}, Ctx: ctx})

  // after
  var invoicePaid = signals.Define[InvoicePaid]("invoice.paid")
  signals.Subscribe(bus, invoicePaid, func(ctx context.Context, p InvoicePaid) error {
      return mail(ctx, p)
  })
  _ = signals.Publish(ctx, bus, invoicePaid, InvoicePaid{...})
  ```

- Replacement, for a subscriber to a model's lifecycle: Quark's hooks
  (`BeforeCreate`, `AfterSave`…) or Quark's event bus, on the Quark model
  that replaces the `pkg/model` one (DEP-2026-024).
- Behavior differences: a typed handler receives the context the event was
  published with (the untyped one carried it inside the event); a payload of
  the wrong shape is an error at subscription time, not a panic in the
  handler.
- Required app changes: the subscription and emission sites.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-025-signals-typed-topics.md`
- Detection rule: `grep -rnE '\.(On|Emit|EmitAsync)\(|signals\.(Event|Handler|Signal)\b' --include='*.go'`;
  staticcheck SA1019 on the markers.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — one `Define` per event name, then the
  subscribe/publish pairs.

### DEP-2026-026 — SQLite stores `time.Time` in a format its date functions read, at v2.0.0

*change · scope `config` (driver behaviour)` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `nucleus/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-026-sqlite-time-format.md`*

**What changes**

A `time.Time` bound to a statement through `drivers/sqlite` (modernc.org/sqlite
with its default DSN) is stored as the text Go's `time.Time.String()`
produces — `2026-10-16 12:30:00 +0000 UTC` — which SQLite's own date
functions do not parse: `date(ts)` over the column is `NULL`, and a query
that filters or groups by date cannot be written in SQL against what the
framework stored (NU-110, seen by Orbit's Data Studio in A11 `O5`). The
driver reads its own text back correctly, so the defect is invisible until
SQL looks at the column.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** nothing in the framework. The way out exists in the
  driver: `_time_format=sqlite` on the DSN (`sqlite://app.db?_time_format=sqlite`)
  makes it write `2026-10-16 12:30:00+00:00`, which `date()` and `strftime()`
  read. This notice and the pinned test say so.
- **v2.0.0:** the framework sets the SQLite format by default on every SQLite
  URL it opens, and reads both forms — rows written before the upgrade stay
  readable. A documented, optional data migration (one `UPDATE` per table
  with a time column) rewrites existing rows for applications that want to
  query them by date.

**How to migrate**

- Replacement: now, add `?_time_format=sqlite` to the SQLite URL in the
  configuration. New rows take the SQLite format; existing rows keep Go's and
  are still read back by the driver. To query old rows by date, rewrite them
  once:

  ```sql
  UPDATE t SET ts = strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%f', substr(ts, 1, 19)) || '+00:00'
   WHERE ts LIKE '% +0000 UTC';
  ```

  (adapted to the zone the rows were written in).
- Behavior differences: at v2.0.0 the stored text changes shape for new rows;
  reading does not change; a tool that parsed the Go text itself must accept
  the SQLite text.
- Required app changes: one DSN parameter now, none at the upgrade; the data
  migration only where date queries over old rows matter.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Assistant spec: `docs/migration_assistants/MA-2026-026-sqlite-time-format.md`
- Detection rule: `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE ts LIKE '% +0000 UTC'` (or
  the zone used) on each table with a time column; a SQLite URL without
  `_time_format`.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — the DSN parameter, then the optional
  `UPDATE`.


## orbit

### DEP-2026-001 — the node identity is bound to the certificate by default at v2.0.0

*change · scope `behaviour` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `orbit/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-001-node-identity-bound-to-certificate-by-default.md`*

**What changes**

An agent listener that verifies client certificates (`--agent-client-ca`)
knows who holds the certificate; it does not, by itself, decide which node
that is. Today the server registers the `node_id` the agent declares and logs
a WARN when it differs from the certificate's Common Name — an agent holding
a certificate for `node-a` can sit in the fleet as `node-b` (OR-57, born in
the A9 arc). `server.Config.AgentIdentityFromCertificate`
(`--agent-identity-from-cert`) binds the two: a registration whose `node_id`
is not the verified Common Name is refused with `PermissionDenied`. It is
opt-in because a fleet that shares one certificate across its agents would
stop registering the day the default changed, and a published default does
not change within `v1.x`.

The owner decided that the binding is the default at the major, and that a
fleet which shares a certificate says so instead of relying on the default.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** `server.Config.AllowSharedAgentCertificate`
  (`--allow-shared-agent-certificate`, env
  `NUCLEUS_ADMIN_ALLOW_SHARED_AGENT_CERTIFICATE=1`) is added. It keeps
  registering the declared `node_id` when it is not the certificate's Common
  Name — today's regime — and keeps it across the major. It contradicts
  `AgentIdentityFromCertificate`, so `Run` refuses to start with both set. A
  listener that verifies client certificates with **neither** field set
  starts as before and logs one WARN at start naming the two fields, so the
  deployment chooses in its own time rather than at the upgrade. A mismatch
  is still logged as a WARN per registration, with both identities: tolerated,
  never silent.
- **v2.0.0:** a listener that verifies client certificates binds the node
  identity to the certificate unless `AllowSharedAgentCertificate` is set: a
  registration whose `node_id` is not the Common Name is refused with
  `PermissionDenied`, as `AgentIdentityFromCertificate` does today.
  `AgentIdentityFromCertificate` keeps its meaning (on a listener that does
  not verify certificates it still refuses to start); setting it is no longer
  necessary under mutual TLS. Nothing changes for a listener that does not
  verify client certificates: there is no certificate to bind to.

**At 2.0**

| Deployment | Today | At `v2.0.0` |
|---|---|---|
| `--agent-client-ca`, neither flag | registers the declared `node_id`, WARN per mismatch, WARN at start naming the two flags | **refuses** a `node_id` that is not the Common Name (`PermissionDenied`) |
| `--agent-client-ca --agent-identity-from-cert` | refuses the mismatch | refuses the mismatch (unchanged) |
| `--agent-client-ca --allow-shared-agent-certificate` | registers the declared `node_id`, WARN per mismatch | registers the declared `node_id`, WARN per mismatch (unchanged) |
| both flags | refuses to start | refuses to start (unchanged) |
| no client-certificate verification | registers the declared `node_id` | registers the declared `node_id` (unchanged) |

**How to migrate**

- **Now (v1):** decide, per server, and write it down in its configuration.
  Either is quiet at start; the decision is what the WARN asks for.

  ```sh
  # one certificate per node, named after it — the recommended posture
  admin-server --agent-client-ca ca.pem --agent-cert s.pem --agent-key s.key \
    --agent-identity-from-cert

  # a fleet whose agents share one certificate: say so, and keep it at 2.0
  admin-server --agent-client-ca ca.pem --agent-cert s.pem --agent-key s.key \
    --allow-shared-agent-certificate
  ```

  In Go: `server.Config{AgentIdentityFromCertificate: true}` or
  `server.Config{AllowSharedAgentCertificate: true}`.
- **At 2.0:** a server with `--agent-client-ca` and neither flag binds. The
  agents it served must present a certificate whose Common Name is their
  `node_id` — an agent whose certificate comes from files and that sets no
  `node_id` already does.
- **Behaviour differences, from the operator's side:** at the major, an agent
  that registered under a name other than its certificate's drops out of the
  fleet with `PermissionDenied` on the stream, logged by the server with both
  names. Nothing else changes: the refusal is the one
  `--agent-identity-from-cert` applies today.
- **Required changes:** one flag, or one certificate per node.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- At start, the server logs
  `agent listener verifies client certificates but does not bind node identity to them`
  with the hint naming `DEP-2026-001` and both flags: this server has not
  chosen.
- Per registration, `admin agent registered under a node_id that differs from its client certificate`
  with `node_id` and `certificate_cn`: this fleet relies on the regime that
  changes. A fleet that never logs it is not affected either way.
- In configuration: `grep -E 'agent-identity-from-cert|allow-shared-agent-certificate|AGENT_IDENTITY_FROM_CERT|ALLOW_SHARED_AGENT_CERTIFICATE'`
  over the unit files and environment files of each `admin-server`; a server
  with `--agent-client-ca` and no hit is the one to decide for.

**What breaks if ignored**

At `v2.0.0`, on a server that verifies client certificates and sets neither
flag, every agent whose declared `node_id` is not its certificate's Common
Name is refused at registration and disappears from the fleet views; its
events, snapshots and Data Studio requests stop with it. The server says why,
once per attempt, with both names. A fleet whose certificates already name
their nodes notices nothing.

### DEP-2026-002 — the Nucleus data-source adapter leaves at v2.0.0

*removal · scope `api` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-01-17 · source: `orbit/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-002-nucleus-datasource-adapter-leaves.md`*

**What changes**

Data Studio speaks Orbit's neutral `datasource` contract. The panel and the
fleet agent fill it, by default, with the Nucleus adapter
(`github.com/jcsvwinston/orbit/datasource/nucleus`): the one place in Orbit
that imports `nucleus/pkg/model` and `pkg/db`, wrapping the application's
model registry, its database handles and `model.NewCRUD`. An application
that runs the Quark ORM hands the panel a `quarkdatasource` adapter instead,
through `orbit.Config.DataSource` (and `agent.Config.DataSource` or
`ExtensionConfig.DataSource` on a fleet node).

Nucleus retires `pkg/model` as a public data layer at its 2.0 (Nucleus
`DEP-2026-024`): Quark is the data layer of the suite, and the framework
stops carrying a second one. The owner decided on 2026-10-16 that the Orbit
adapter built on it leaves with it, rather than being kept on a demoted
substrate: at 2.0 the panel reads Quark models only, through
`quarkdatasource`.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** the package, `Config`, `Adapter` and `New` carry
  `// Deprecated:`; everything keeps working. An application that mounts the
  panel without `orbit.Config.DataSource`, and a fleet node that runs the
  agent with a registry and no `DataSource`, log one WARN at start naming
  this notice and the way to stay.
- **v2.0.0:** the package is removed. `orbit.Config.DataSource` is required:
  a nil value is a configuration error, and the module refuses to start
  naming it, the way it refuses an action on a model that does not exist. An
  agent with no `DataSource` serves no Data Studio on that node (as a node
  with no registry does today). The runtime field-metadata editor
  (`PUT /api/models/{name}/schema/fields`, `PanelConfig.SchemaRegistry`)
  leaves with the adapter: it mutates the Nucleus registry, has no
  equivalent in the contract, and a panel on a custom source already
  answers it with `501`. The `*signals.Bus` the adapter hands to
  `model.NewCRUD` (`Config.Bus`, the panel's `SetSignalBus`) leaves with it
  too — Nucleus `DEP-2026-025` names Orbit as the holder of that bus through
  the untyped door, and nothing else in Orbit uses that door.

**How to migrate**

- **Now (v1):** define the models with Quark and mount the panel on the
  Quark adapter. The panel's own tables (operators, sessions, audit) are not
  models of the source and need nothing.

  ```go
  // before: the default — Data Studio over the application's pkg/model registry
  app := nucleus.New().
      Use("orbit", orbit.Module(orbit.Config{Prefix: "/admin"}))

  // after: Data Studio over Quark models, through the adapter that stays
  src := quarkdatasource.New(provider) // the application's quark.ClientProvider
  if err := quarkdatasource.Register[Article](src); err != nil {
      log.Fatal(err)
  }
  app := nucleus.New().
      Use("orbit", orbit.Module(orbit.Config{Prefix: "/admin", DataSource: src}))

  // a fleet node: the same adapter, on the agent
  agent.NewExtension(agent.ExtensionConfig{Endpoints: endpoints, DataSource: src}, stateDir, version)
  ```

  The quick start (`website/docs/quick-start.md`, step 4, *With the Quark
  ORM*) shows this path beside the default one. The adapter's README
  (`quarkdatasource/README.md`: *Usage*, *In the fleet*, *Semantics*)
  names the options it takes (`WithTenantColumn`,
  `WithDatabaseAlias`) and what it answers: the filter operators, a missing
  row as a `404`, a record it cannot write as a `422` per field, and the
  tenant scoping it applies. The *Data Studio* section of the features page
  says how the two adapters differ on validation, search and counts.
- **At 2.0:** an application that still passes no `DataSource` does not
  start; the error names the field. There is no Nucleus adapter to fall back
  to, because there is no `pkg/model` registry to read.
- **Behaviour differences:** Quark counts exactly where the Nucleus adapter
  may estimate (`CountResult.IsEstimated` is false), applies its own version
  checks and tenant scoping, and the field-metadata editor is not available
  (it mutates the Nucleus registry, which a Quark source does not have; the
  panel answers `501` for it today on any custom source).
- **Required app changes:** the model definitions (Quark instead of
  `pkg/model`, which Nucleus's own notice covers) and one field on
  `orbit.Config` — or on the agent's configuration on a fleet node.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- At start, the panel logs
  `orbit: Data Studio reads the application's pkg/model registry through the Nucleus adapter, which leaves at Orbit 2.0 (DEP-2026-002)`,
  and a fleet node logs the same with the `admin agent:` prefix. An
  application that does not log it is already on its own source.
- Source scan: `grep -rn 'orbit/datasource/nucleus"' --include='*.go' .` for
  a direct use of the adapter; a composition root with `orbit.Module(` and no
  `DataSource:` for the default; staticcheck SA1019 on the markers.
- Suggested rewrite: manual — the model layer moves to Quark first.

**What breaks if ignored**

At `v2.0.0`, an application that mounts the panel with a nil
`orbit.Config.DataSource` does not start, and a fleet node with a registry
and no `DataSource` serves no Data Studio. Code that imports
`orbit/datasource/nucleus` does not compile. Nothing changes for an
application already on `quarkdatasource`.

### DEP-2026-003 — an operator with no tenant is refused in a multi-tenant application at v2.0.0

*change · scope `behaviour` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-02-07 · source: `orbit/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-003-operators-must-be-bound-to-a-tenant.md`*

**What changes**

With `multitenant_enabled` on, Data Studio is confined to the tenant the host
application resolves for each request. Until this release that was the only
input: the operator account had no tenant, so the panel confined an operator
to whatever tenant the request resolved. With Nucleus' `header` resolver the
tenant is the value of a header the client sends, and a plain operator of one
tenant — no superuser rights, no `tenant_switch` — who was refused
`?tenant=<other>` listed, exported, read by id and created rows in the other
tenant by naming it in the header (OR-80). The `tenant_switch` gate and its
`tenant.override` audit entry covered `?tenant=` only.

The operator account now carries a tenant (`tenant_id`, a nullable column of
`nucleus_admin_users`). An operator who is bound to one is confined to it by
the panel itself, whatever the request resolves. The owner listed the binding
for the major: in a multi-tenant application every operator who is not a
superuser and holds no `tenant_switch` is bound to a tenant, and one who is
not is refused rather than left to the resolver.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** the column, the `tenant_id` field of the operator API,
  and the confinement. A bound operator who may not switch tenants works in
  their tenant only: a request that resolves another tenant — from the header,
  the subdomain or `?tenant=` — is refused with `403`, reads and writes alike;
  a request that resolves no tenant gets theirs, ahead of
  `multitenant_default`. An operator with **no** tenant keeps today's
  behaviour — the resolver decides — and the panel logs one WARN per operator
  per process naming this notice and how to set the tenant. A superuser or a
  `tenant_switch` holder is not confined by the tenant on their account; the
  switching rules, and the audit of every switch, are unchanged.
- **v2.0.0:** in a multi-tenant application, a request from an operator with
  no tenant, who is not a superuser and holds no `tenant_switch`, is refused
  with `403` naming the missing tenant. A bound operator, a superuser and a
  `tenant_switch` holder behave as in this release.

Refused rather than silently confined: the host has already scoped the
request to the tenant it resolved (its database alias, its storage prefix),
and answering it with another tenant's rows would mix the two. The refusal is
the one `?tenant=` naming another tenant has answered since OR-23.

**At 2.0**

| Operator, `multitenant_enabled` on | Today | At `v2.0.0` |
|---|---|---|
| bound to a tenant, may not switch | confined to it; a request resolving another tenant is `403` | unchanged |
| **no tenant**, may not switch | follows the tenant each request resolves; one WARN per process | **`403`** on every request to the panel |
| superuser or `tenant_switch`, with or without a tenant | the resolver's tenant; `?tenant=` allowed and audited | unchanged |
| any, `multitenant_enabled` off | not confined | unchanged |

**How to migrate**

- **Now (v1):** give every operator who is not a superuser and holds no
  `tenant_switch` the tenant they work in. From the panel's API, as an
  operator with `operators_manage` on `admin:*`:

  ```http
  PUT /admin/api/admin-users/<id>
  Content-Type: application/json

  {"tenant_id": "acme"}
  ```

  or at creation, with `"tenant_id"` in the `POST /admin/api/admin-users`
  body. `nucleus createuser` has no tenant flag: set the tenant of an operator
  it created through the API afterwards, or in the table
  (`UPDATE nucleus_admin_users SET tenant_id = 'acme' WHERE username = 'ana'`).
  Write the tenant as the host resolves it: Nucleus lower-cases the tenant
  it reads from a header or a subdomain, and the panel compares tenants
  exactly. An operator who genuinely works across tenants gets
  `tenant_switch` on `admin:*` instead, and every switch they make is
  audited.
- **At 2.0:** an operator left without a tenant and without either right is
  refused by the panel; nothing else changes for them or anyone else.
- **Behaviour differences, from the operator's side:** once bound, an
  operator who relied on the header or the subdomain to reach another tenant
  gets `403` there. That is the defect this closes; the tenant they are bound
  to works as before, and a request that resolves no tenant now opens their
  tenant instead of being refused.
- **Required changes:** one value per affected operator account.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- In the log, once per operator per process:
  `orbit: operator has no tenant in a multi-tenant application ...` with
  `operator`, `operator_id` and a `hint` naming the API call. An operator who
  never logs it is not affected.
- In the table, the candidates:

  ```sql
  SELECT id, username FROM nucleus_admin_users
   WHERE is_active = 1 AND is_superuser = 0
     AND (tenant_id IS NULL OR tenant_id = '');
  ```

  minus the ones holding `tenant_switch` (or `*`) on `admin:*`, directly or
  through a role (`GET /admin/api/rbac/policies`).

**What breaks if ignored**

At `v2.0.0`, in an application with `multitenant_enabled` on, every operator
with no tenant who is not a superuser and holds no `tenant_switch` can no
longer use the panel: each request answers `403`, naming the missing tenant.
Operators who are bound, superusers and `tenant_switch` holders notice
nothing.

### DEP-2026-004 — `system_pulse` stops including the process environment at v2.0.0

*change · scope `behaviour` (permissions)` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-02-07 · source: `orbit/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-004-system-pulse-drops-the-environment.md`*

**What changes**

The system snapshot (`GET <prefix>/api/system/snapshot`, behind the panel's
System and Overview screens) carries the process environment in its
`environment` field, and the snapshot is authorized by one action,
`system_pulse` on `admin:*`. Values whose name looks secret-bearing (`*URL*`,
`*TOKEN*`, `*PASS*`, `*KEY*`, `*AUTH*`, …) are masked and URL credentials
are redacted, but the rest is served in clear: on the host the re-audit
measured, 58 of 70 variables (`HOME`, `PATH`, `USER`, `TMPDIR` and, on
that host, an email address). An operator granted
`system_pulse` to watch goroutines and the connection pool reads all of it.

The environment moves to its own action, **`system_env`** on `admin:*`.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** `system_env` exists. A superuser, or an operator who
  holds `system_pulse` **and** `system_env`, reads the environment exactly as
  before. An operator who holds `system_pulse` without `system_env` still
  reads it — today's behaviour, unchanged — and the panel logs one WARN the
  first time that operator does so in the process, naming `DEP-2026-004`,
  the operator and the action to grant. The snapshot is polled by the
  Overview and System screens, so the WARN is once per operator per process,
  not per request. `system_env` widens `system_pulse` and opens nothing on
  its own: without `system_pulse` the snapshot answers `403`, as today.
- **v2.0.0:** an operator who holds `system_pulse` without `system_env` gets
  the snapshot with `"environment": []`. Everything else in the snapshot
  stays under `system_pulse`. The WARN goes away with the behaviour it
  announces.

**At 2.0**

| Operator | Today | At `v2.0.0` |
|---|---|---|
| superuser | environment | environment (unchanged) |
| `system_pulse` and `system_env` | environment | environment (unchanged) |
| `system_pulse` only | environment, one WARN per operator per process | **`"environment": []`**, no WARN |
| `system_env` only | `403` on the snapshot | `403` on the snapshot (unchanged) |
| neither | `403` on the snapshot | `403` on the snapshot (unchanged) |
| open posture (no auth provider) | environment | environment (unchanged) |

**How to migrate**

- **Now (v1):** decide who needs the environment and grant them
  `system_env` on `admin:*`. The operators who only watch the runtime need
  nothing; the WARN names each operator who reads the environment without
  it, so the log is the list to decide on.

  From the panel's Access Control screen, the policy
  `(ops, admin:*, system_env)` — the screen posts
  `{"sub":"ops","obj":"admin:*","act":"system_env"}` to
  `<prefix>/api/rbac/policies`. In Go, on the application's authorizer:

  ```go
  enf.AddPolicy("ops", "admin:*", "system_env")
  ```

  In a Casbin policy file: `p, ops, admin:*, system_env`. An application
  with its own `AdminAuth` provider and no enforcer answers
  `Authorize(user, "*", "system_env")`.
- **At 2.0:** nothing to do for an operator granted `system_env`. An
  operator without it sees an empty environment list.
- **Behaviour differences, from the operator's side:** at the major, an
  operator with `system_pulse` alone sees the snapshot without the
  environment. A client that reads `environment` gets an empty array, never
  `null` and never a missing field.
- **Required changes:** one policy row per subject that needs the
  environment, or none.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- At runtime, the panel logs
  `orbit: the system snapshot serves the process environment to an operator without system_env; system_pulse stops including it at Orbit 2.0 (DEP-2026-004)`
  with `operator_id`, `operator`, `role` and a `hint` naming `system_env`,
  once per operator per process. A panel that never logs it is not affected.
- In the policies: the subjects granted `system_pulse` on `admin:*` without
  `system_env` (or `*`) are the ones the change reaches —
  `GET <prefix>/api/rbac/policies`, or
  `grep -E 'system_pulse|system_env' policy.csv`.

**What breaks if ignored**

At `v2.0.0`, an operator granted `system_pulse` without `system_env` sees
the System screen without the environment, and a script that reads
`environment` from the snapshot under such an account gets an empty list.
Nothing else in the snapshot changes, and no request that succeeds today is
refused.

### DEP-2026-005 — the mesh accepts only configured peers at v2.0.0

*change · scope `behaviour` · v2.0.0, no earlier than 2027-02-07 · source: `orbit/docs/deprecations/DEP-2026-005-mesh-accepts-only-configured-peers.md`*

**What changes**

Servers of a fleet speak to each other on their agent listeners: each one
dials the endpoints in its `--peers` and opens `PeerService.Sync`, and the
other side records what it hears — the peer's nodes in its registry, its
events in its bus and replay. Today the receiving side asks nothing beyond
the agent listener's own authentication, and `PeerService` is mounted on
every server, peers configured or not. A holder of the agent token, or of
any certificate the agents' CA signed, can open `Sync`, announce a server
that does not exist, and list nodes and relay events attributed to any
`node_id` to every operator of that server.

`server.Config.PeerAllowlist` (`--peer-allowlist`) closes it: a peer is
accepted only when it is a server this one dials, and under mutual TLS
only when its certificate names it. It is opt-in in `v1.x` because a
fleet whose servers do not all list each other would lose the links the
missing entries carry the day the default changed, and a published default
does not change within `v1.x`.

At the major every server applies the check.

What changes and when:

- **This release:** `server.Config.PeerAllowlist` (`--peer-allowlist`, env
  `NUCLEUS_ADMIN_PEER_ALLOWLIST=1`) is added. With it, `Sync` accepts a peer
  only when
  1. the `server_id` it announces is the one that answered on this
     server's own link to one of its `--peers` endpoints — the list names
     endpoints, and dialling one is what says which server sits behind it;
  2. when it arrived with a verified client certificate (an agent listener
     with `--agent-client-ca`), the certificate's Common Name is that
     `server_id`.

  Anything else is refused with `PermissionDenied` and a WARN naming the
  peer and the reason. A server with no `--peers` accepts no peer.
  Without the flag nothing is refused: each peer the check would refuse is
  accepted as before and logged **once per `server_id` per process** as a
  WARN that names this notice and the flag.
- **v2.0.0:** every server applies the check. `PeerAllowlist` and
  `--peer-allowlist` then describe what the server does anyway; they stay
  accepted, so a configuration that sets them keeps starting. There is no
  setting that keeps today's regime: a server that must be a peer is listed
  in `--peers`.

**At 2.0**

| Peer that opens `Sync` | Today, default | Today, `--peer-allowlist` | At `v2.0.0` |
|---|---|---|---|
| a server this one dials (`--peers`), certificate named after it or no certificate | accepted | accepted | accepted (unchanged) |
| a server this one does not dial | accepted, WARN once | **refused** | **refused** |
| a caller with the agent token or an agent certificate, announcing any `server_id` | accepted, WARN once | **refused** — except a token holder announcing the name of a server this one dials (below) | **refused**, same exception |
| a certificate whose Common Name is not the announced `server_id` | accepted, WARN once | **refused** | **refused** |

Without client certificates the check compares names, not credentials: a
holder of the agent token who knows the `server_id` of a server this one
dials can still announce it. Under mutual TLS the certificate decides.

**How to migrate**

- **Now (v1):** make every link a configured one, then turn the check on.

  ```sh
  # each server lists every other server it exchanges nodes with
  admin-server --server-id a --peers https://b.internal:9090 ... --peer-allowlist
  admin-server --server-id b --peers https://a.internal:9090 ... --peer-allowlist
  ```

  Under mutual TLS, name each server's client certificate after its
  `--server-id` (or set `--server-id` to the certificate's Common Name).
  In Go: `server.Config{PeerAddrs: ..., PeerAllowlist: true}`.
- **At 2.0:** nothing more to do for a fleet that ran with the flag.
- **Behaviour differences, from the operator's side:** a server that one
  peer dials and that does not dial it back stops receiving that peer's
  nodes and events: list it in `--peers` on both sides. A peer refused
  logs `admin server: peer refused` with the reason on the refusing server,
  and the link fails with `PermissionDenied` on the dialling one.
- **Required changes:** at most one `--peers` entry per missing direction,
  and certificates named after the servers.

**How to tell you rely on it**

- Per peer, once per process, on a server without the flag:
  `admin server: accepted a peer that Orbit 2.0 refuses` with `peer`,
  `agent_endpoint`, `certificate_cn` and `reason`. A server that never logs
  it is not affected.
- With the flag on, `admin server: peer refused` is what the major will
  refuse; a fleet can run with it in staging first.
- In configuration: `grep -E 'peer-allowlist|PEER_ALLOWLIST'` over the unit
  files and environment files of each `admin-server` with `--peers`.

The announcement is per peer rather than one WARN at start, unlike
`DEP-2026-001`: what changes depends on who connects, which a server does
not know until a peer does.

**What breaks if ignored**

At `v2.0.0`, a server that receives a peer it does not dial, or whose
certificate names another server, refuses the link; the nodes and events
that peer carried disappear from that server's views. The server says
which peer and why on every refused attempt.
